SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state : 
(a) the names of Non-Governmental Organisations in Gujarat which are 
receiving financial assistance from her Ministry; 
(b) whether any review of the working of such organisations has been 
carried out; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether any of the organisation has ever been black-listed; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI): (a) A statement 
is laid on the Table of the House. (See below) 
(b) and(c) Monitoring and evaluation of the pe rformance of the NGOs 
receiving grant -in-aid is carried out through data received from the NGOs 
regarding past performance, inspections by the representations of the State 
Governments, nodal agencies and the Ministry's own officials. The performance 
of the NGOs that have been assisted in the State of Gujarat is by and large 
satisfactory. 
(d) No Sir. 
(e) Does not arise.

[8 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI GOPALSINH G. SOLANKI: Sir, as far as the question of social 
justice and related aspects of NGOs and VOs are concerned, there is a concept 
of service. A work is considered as service when one renders it on his own. At 
the same time, if he takes something, then it is not considered service. As far as 
the comparison of the NGOs of Gujarat with those in the other four States is 
concerned, there were only 28 in 1997 in the State of Gujarat; in 1998-99, there 
were 18; and in 1999- 2000, the release of funds has been to 60 NGOs. For 
Andhra Pradesh, it was 204, 309; and this year, it is 320; for U.P., it was 260, 
338 and 349; for West Bengal, it was 126,167 and 155; and for Karnataka, 
for the year 1992-94, it was 103. I would like to know, when there is no list 
which is blac klisted, then why only 60 NGOs have been sanctioned funds in 
Gujarat? Secondly, as far as the question of girls' hostels are concerned in 
Scheduled Tribe areas, there has not been any release of funds to NGOs this 
year. Why is this so? This is my second supplementary. 
SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI: Sir. for Gujarat, specifically, we gave 
not 18 in 1998-99 but 118; and this year we have given 71. Now the question, 
as I understand is, why it is not as much as it is in Andhra Pradesh or some other 
State? Firstly, because, it really does not depend on us. We don't do suo motu 
finding of NGOs. It depends which NGO has done paper work, how fast they 
are at it, how fast the inspection is done—which is being speeded up in the last 
two years and which is why you see such a quantum jump in the number of 
NGOs getting money—and how much money they want. So. Gujarat has done 
very well. Andhra Pradesh is number one because they send the names of NGOs 
much faster and the State Government takes a great deal of interest in NGO 
referals. The State Governments that don't take an interest in NGO referals you 
will find are correspondingly less. Regarding girls hostels, we have not given 
any girls' hostels because the Gujarat NGOs have not asked for any as yet.  
SHRI GOPALSINH G. SOLANKI: Sir, so far as the question of reviewing 
the performance of the NGOs or getting the report from the NGOs is concerned, 
I would like to say that all NGOs and voluntary organisations have been 
registered under the Public Trusts Act. It is not that under the Public Trust, Act, 
the Commissioner inspects the NGOs. It is only the Chartered Accountant, 
who prepares a report and sends it to the Charity Commissioner every year. 
The question of review is very much left out. At the same time, NGOs and 
voluntary organisations, which are required to be blacklisted, arc not blacklisted 
in time. Therefore, I would like to know (a) On the question of blacklisting in 
the whole nation, as compared to Gujarat, how many   NGOs have been 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [8 MAY. 2000] 
blacklisted, particularly in Bihar. UP. West Bengal and Madhya Pradesh: (b) 
So far as the Gujarat State is concerned why the amount has not been released 
vet: (c) If you look at the list of all the NGOs in the statement attached to the 
answer, you find that they are all based in the urban areas. Therefore. I would 
like to know whether the hon. Minister would try to get the registration done in 
rural parts of the nation since the beneficiaries are in the rural areas. 
SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI: I will try to respond to the questions. 
The hon. Member said that the Charity Commissioner inspects the NGOs, but 
this is not correct. The Social Welfare Department of the State Government 
mpects them. We now have a double inspecting system. I have retired Army 
officers; I have reputed agencies like CRY, Helpage. and I have a large number 
of social service institutes that are recognised and run by the Government or 
which have national recognition like the TISS in Bombay, They do inspection 
in the areas that are specifically allocated to them. 
The second thing we have done is, we have found that when the inspection 
was being done, they really did not know what they were looking for. They 
would go and ask superficial questions; like for instance they would ask : Do 
you have an airconditioner?' In an area where is no electricity or where there is 
very little electricity and where nobody else has an airconditioner. What we 
have done is, in the process, we are making it a specific inspection report, specific 
review reports, so that the inspector also would not deviate and apply his own 
logic to it. This is with regard to the first part. 
As to the second part, it is a pertinent point raised by the hon. Member. 
I have brought it up myself. The NGOs that we give to, we give mainly to 
urban areas. For instance, in Gujarat, it is Ahmedabad and Baroda, which have 
taken a large share, with a little bit in Surat. It is quite true that they are urban 
based. But if you look at what they do, very litle work is done in the cities. Most 
of the beneficiarie s are in the rural areas, but the NGOs address is an urban 
address. The third question is which are the ones which are blacklisted. So far 
there are 19 NGOs which are blacklisted—Uttar Pradesh tops the list with 12, 
Bihar with 6, West Bengal 2, Orissa with 1, Tamil Nadu with 1, and Maharashtra 
1. That is all. 
SHRI BRAHMAKUMAR BHATT : Sir, I would like to know whether 
the hon. Minister has visited any of these organisations in Gujarat. Is it a fact 
that all these NGOs in Gujarat have been working for several  years and some 
of them have been working even for several decades?  Sir, these organisations 
14 

[8 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
are working particularly in the rural areas outside the city of Ahmedabad, but 
their headquarters are in Ahmedabad. These organisations are run by responsible 
social workers of longstanding experience who are doing a good work. I would 
like to know whether it is a fact and what the experience and opinion of the hon. 
Minister is in this regard. 
SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI: Sir, I will actually go by the opinion 
that everybody in India should be responsible lest it is proved otherwise. We 
have sent people for inspection. The State Government has inspected. Sir, the 
NGOs of Gujarat whom we give money are by and large good people. They do 
a lot of good work. However, this Ministry is always open to complaints. Every 
single complaint that we get, we investigate. You did not put this question but 
I am voluntarily giving this information that I do not know what to do other 
than stopping the funds. We are trying to work out a way in which we can ask 
the State Governments to actually recover the funds from those people who 
have been defaulting and who do not exist on the ground. In some cases, we 
have found cases of forged signatures especially in Madh ya Pradesh, we have 
found that the NGOs simply do not exist. What I have asked the people of my 
Ministry to do from this month onwards is— there are 10 to 15 designated officers 
in my Ministry — to take one State and spend there four days to look for the 
agencies about which even there is the slightest suspicion. The first thing is the 
forged recommendation. Secondly, sometimes we get recommendation from 
those people who are Government servants and who have realised that it is easy 
to fill in the form and they know the right people. Thirdly, sometimes, I hesitate 
to say, perhaps, MPs recommending NGOs from their own constituencies which 
simply do not exist. Fourthly, for instance, somebody starts a deaf and dumb 
school. It is a school and we give money continuously. After three or four years 
I have started asking them as to how many children have passed the examinations, 
not as to how many children are in the school. In one case we found that they 
had failed year after year. In that case we will cancel the grant. Obviously, it is 
not doing its work. I am still trying to work out something which actually conveys 
as a deterrent for those people who are not responsible.

SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI : Sir, as I sa id, it is quite true that a 
large number of these NGOs are in Ahmedabad and cities like that. As 1 also 
said, their beneficiaries are outside the city. However in regard to the specific 
programme for street children, I would like to submit that we have started it in 
nine cities. We did extremely well. We had rescued thousands of children. We 
are now extending it to thirty more cities. But this can only be a city -based 
programme because we really come across street children in cities. The children 
either come on their own or they are being sold to someone or they come to 
work in cities. They are mistreated in cities because of which they find 
themselves helpless and, therefore, the Street Children Programme has to be a 
city-based and a town-based programme. 
Secondly, in the revised guidelines, as I told you, we are giving preference 
to people who work in the rural areas. After the guidelines are made, it is up to 
each Member of Parliament or an NGO to get people together to do work in the 
rural areas and then apply to us for funds. We will be happy to fund them. 
SHRIKULDIP NAYYAR: Sir, I am associated with an NGO organisation 
called the Citizens for Democracy. We found that after the defeat of the Janta 
Party in 1980, we were very much harassed. Now, again we f ind, during the 
last one year, we have been harassed by the Government. Sir, even though we 
have the income-tax exemption certificate, still, we are being asked to produce 
all kinds of papers dating back to ten or twelve years. Not only this; a number 
of inspectors are coming. I would like to know from the Minister whether it is 
the policy of the Government to harass those organisations which do not fall in 
line with their political thinking. 
SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI : I am afraid, the Citizens for 
Democracy is not applied to me for anything. I have a very limited mandate 
and that is education, minorities, etc. It is on a huge mandate on which I release 
funds to the NGOs at large. 
16 

[8 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Secondly, it is not the Government's policy to harass the NGOs; at least 
it is not the policy of my Ministry because I myself come with an NGO 
background. 
DR. Y. RADHAKRISHNA MURTY : Sir. recently, there was an 
interesting observation made in a journal about the NGOs in India. An article 
has been published in a prestigious journal— Economic and Political Weekly. 
The article says, "India's recent experience shows that most of the NGOs are 
elitist organisations far removed from the people. They are basically DONGOS 
i.e. the Donor -driven Organisations who will  collapse as soon as the foreign 
money is withdrawn and the GONGOS — the Government -driven 
Organisations— which are captured by bureaucrats or their wives and, quite 
often, by the wives of Ministers." This is the observation that had been made. I 
would like to know the reaction from the Minister on this. 
SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI : It is an interesting observation. But 
it is very outdated. This is the view that was held during the sixties. I would 
like to explain a few things. The first one is, the Government cannot reach out 
to lot of places and in many, many cases, specially, in the social welfare wings. 
the Government abdicates its responsibility to a large extent. We, then, prefer 
to rely on people who know the local conditions, work locally and, I believe the 
NGOs fill the niche which the Government will never be able to step in 
because they are much more closely connected with the community. As far as 
the Donor -driven Organisations are concerned, it is quite true that some of 
them are donor-driven, But why no t? If we can give money to meet two bad 
things, we can give money to do two good things as well. You have a person 
putting in his time in this country. So, do we not put value on his time? Do we 
not put an economic value on his time? The fact that this per son is giving his 
life to teach street children or to go out of his way to look after lepers. We 
should put an economic value on his time and measure it in far greater terms, 
than giving Rs. 2 lakhs or Rs. 3 lakhs and harass them for huge amounts of 
paper work. Sometimes, running schools have to be shut down because we do 
not give the second instalment. So, I see no reason why they should not be 
donor-driven or Government-driven. However, we have taken a policy decision 
in my Ministry that those NGOs that we find capable of standing on their own 
feet, after three years, we will slowly and slowly —say, 10 per cent or 20 per 
cent, at a time— decrease their grant and divert them to people who need it. For 
instance, in Bastar, it has to be donor-driven because there is no local support, 
in terms of money. There are no rich people. There is nobody to give money. 
 17 

RAJYA SABHA |8 MAY, 2000] 
So, obviously, the Government is going to support them because my ultimate 
aim is that the benefit should reach the poorest of the poor. So. Sir, as I said, I 
see no reason why, in some areas of this country, they should not be donor -
driven; whether it is foreign money or Indian money, money is money.

*582. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SURYA': Will the Minister of YOUTH 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether there is any scheme for indentifying talented players; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government are considering any  proposal under the said 
scheme for the persons belonging to the Scheduled Tribe keeping in view their 
capabilities; and 
(d) whether Government will consider organizing tribal sports competition 
on all India basis like the rural sport? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AF FAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI 
SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of 
the House. 
STATEMENT 
Scheme to Spot Talented Players 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Under the scheme of 'National Sports Talent Contest' talented school 
children in the age of 9— 12 are identified. Children are selected in 15disciplines

through a 'Battery of tests' and contests held at different levels. Following 
selection, these children are admitted in 57 schools adopted by Sports Authority 
of India where their board, lodging, and tuition fees etc. are met fully by the 
Government. Besides, under the scheme of Rural Sports Programmes District, 
State and National level sports championships are organised and talented sports 
players are spotted and selected for further coaching and training for National 
and International competitions. Under the scheme, North -East Sports Festival 
is organised to tap the hidden talent which is in abundance in the region. 
(c) The schemes mentioned above are implemented for all sports persons 
including those belonging to Scheduled Tribes Besides, the scheme of Special 
Area Games (SAG) which was launched in 1985, caters to scouting of natural 
talent from tribal, hilly, rural and c oastal areas, keeping in view the physical 
attributes of the people required for a particular sports. The scouted talent is 
imparted scientific training to meet the demands of modern competitive games 
and sports so as to attain excellence. 
(d) There is no move  to have on All India tribal sports competition. 
However, there is a North-East Sports Festival held every year where a majority 
of the participants are Tribal.

Problems faced by Tea Industry 
*591. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE : Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is fact that the Tea Industry in India is currently facing 
serious problems all round; 
(b) if so the, details thereof; and 
(c) what steps are proposed to be taken to help the industry to face these 
challenges ? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
MURASOLI MARAN): (a) and (b) After a year of shortfall in production and 
exports in 1999, the tea  industry is currently showing improvement on the 
production front. Production of tea during January and February 2000 was 37.72 
million kgs as compared to 36.23 million kgs in the corresponding period of 
the previous year. However, tea indusrty has suffer ed a set back in exports as 
well as in prices fetched at auction during the same period. 
(c) Several steps have been taken by the Government/Tea Board for 
increasing production and export of tea. The steps taken to increase production 
include financial assistance by Tea Board to the tea industry through its various 
developmental schemes for encouraging extension planting, re -planting, 
rejuvenation pruning, infilling, creation of irrigation facilities and drainage etc. 
44 

[8 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
With a vi ew to promote export of tea Government and the Tea Board 
have been analysing country- wise exports of tea giving special attention to 
areas offering potential. Tea Board also acts to remove bottlenecks in exports 
to individual markets whenever these are noticed. Certain other steps taken to 
increase exports of tea include : 
(i) participation in major trade fairs/exhibitions abroad; 
(ii) field sampling at speciality stores and in princinal markets. 
(in) media campaign to increase consumer awareness of the speciality of 
Indian teas and to popularise the Tea Board marketing symbol which 
stands for pure Indian tea. 
(iv) exchange of tea delegations between India and tea importing countries. 
With a view to compensate the small growers of tea for the low prices at 
the auctions, Government has implemented a Scheme through the Tea Board 
for providing subsidy for an amount equal to the shortfall between the auction 
price and Rs. 55 per kg. The extent of such subsidy will be limited to a maximum 
of Rs. 5 per kg of tea or to the extent it is less than Rs. 55 per kg at the auctions 
whichever is less.

WTO Agreement 
4419. Shri K. RAHMAN KHAN : Will the Minister of COMMERCE  
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state : 
(a) Whether it is a fact that the WTO Agreement is a ploy of the developed 
countries to further exploit the developing countries; 
(b) if so, what initiatives Government have taken to unite the developing 
countries and ensure protection of national interests of our country as well as of 
the developing countries; and 
(c) what is the outcome thereof ? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (MURASOLI 
MARAN) : (a) WTO Agreements have benefited India and other developing 
countries in as much as a rule based, transpa rent and predictable multilateral 
trading system is essential to ensure effective market access for developing 
countries like India, who are not a major force in global trade due to their small 
share, besides being the sine qua non for the effective exploitation of trading 
60 

[8 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
opportunities. The WTO Agreements were a package where some provisions 
have benefited us, whlie others have imposed onerous obligations. An open, 
fair and rule based trading system is in the interest of developing countries like 
India, as it protects Members from unilateral action by stronger trading partners. 
In this connection it may be noted that several developing countries, including 
China, are currently seeking accession to WTO. 
(b) To graner support for the Indian stand on various issues at WTO, 
India has coordinated with important developing country groupings, such as 
the SAARC, the G -15 and the G -77. Our proposal for implementation issues 
have been tabled in the WTO jointly with 11 other likeminded Group of 
developing countries. In the Third Ministerial Conference of WTO, held at 
Seattle between 30th November to 3rd December, 1999, India's call for upfront 
redressal of the implementation concerns of developing countries and opposition 
to the linkage of trade with core labour standards etc., received support of a 
number of developing countries. As part of post-Seattle efforts, India has actively 
participated as a member of the G -77 Group in the X Session of the United 
Nations Conference on Trade and Development, held at Bangkok during 12-19 
February, 2000, wherein a Plan of Action was adopted which incorporates the 
main concerns of the developing countires. 
(c) At the Seattle Ministerial Conference of WTO, India had effectively 
opposed the linkage of trade with core labour standards and attempts for the 
further expansion of the linkage between trade and environment in the WTO. It 
also created pressure for the early redressal of implementation problems being 
experienced by the developing countries. The Seattl e Ministerial Conference, 
however, could reach no conclusions due to wide divergence of views between 
Members. The Government are continuing efforts for building up solidarity 
with other likeminded developing countries with a view to facilitate effective 
projection and protection of Indian national interest in WTO.

THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
MURASOLI MARAN): (a) Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) flow from America 
has generally been showing an increasing trend except two dips in 1994 and 
1998. 
(b) The inflow of FDI is largely dependent on factors such as commercial 
judgement of the investors, global market conditions and trade fundamentals. 
(c) America rank at Nos. 2 for the inflow of investments. 
(d) With a view to attracting more FDI, the FDI Policy has recently been 
further liberalised and is being continuously reviewed so as to make it both 
attractive and investor friendly and to boost the inflows of FDI and technology 
in the country. 
(e) The details are given in the Statement. 
STATEMENT 
Government, in its commitment towards economic reforms, have 
announced the new Foreign Direct investment (FDI) Policy thereby placing 
all items/activities under the automatic route for Foreign Direct investment (FDI) 
Non-Resident Indians (NRI) and Overseas Corp orate body (OCB) investment 
except the following :—  
1.    All proposals that require an Industrial Licence which include (i) the 
item requiring an industrial Licence under the Industries

being more than 24% in the equity capital of units manufacturing 
items reserved for small scale industries ; and (iii) all items which 
require an Industrial Licence in terms of the locational policy notified

2. All proposals in which the foreign collaborator has a previous venture/ 
tie-up in India. 
3. All proposals relating to acquisition of shares in an existing Indian 
company in favour of a foreign /NRI/OCB   investor. 
4. All proposals falling outside notifed sectoral policy/caps or under 
sectors in which FDI is not permitted and/or whenever any investor 
chooses to make an application to the FIPB and not to avail of the

Removal of Restrictions on Import and Export 
4454. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH : Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state : 
(a) Whether it is a fact that India had removed restrictions on the import 
and export trade policy but the U.S.A. had not removed its restrictions against 
India. 
(b) whether it is als o a fact that the new export -import policy of the 
Government and special zones created thereunder are under fire; 
(c) if answers to parts(a) and (b) above be in the affirmative, what are 
the reasons therefor; and 
(d) what remedial measures Government are taking in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
MURASOLI MARAN) : (a) to (d) India has been following a continuous policy 
of removal of restrictions on imports since 1991. Tariff line-wise import polic 
was first announced on 31-3-1996. As on that date import of 6161 tariff line 
(at 10 digit level) out of the total number of 10202 tariff lines (at 10 digit level, 
was free. Import restrictions on 488 tariff lines (at 10 digit level) were removed 
during the period 1-4-96 to 31-3-97. Further 391 tariff lines (at 8 digit level) 
were freed during the period 1-4-97 to 13-4-98 and 894 tariff lines (at 8 digit 
level) were freed on 1-4-99. Thus removal of import restrictions on 714 tariff 
line as carried out on 31-3-2000 was nothing but the continuation of the stated 
policy of the Government over the years. 
Under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), 1947 all 
Members were obliged to remove all the Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) 
maintained on imports. India, being a Founder Member, was also oblig ed to 
remove the QRs but it took recourse to the exception provided in GATT for 
maintaining such QRs owing to balance of payments (BoP) difficulties. 
However, since 1995, with substantial improvement in India's BoP position, 
certain Members questioned India's continued justification for maintaining QRs 
on BoP grounds. India could negotiate with all other trading partners, with the 
89 

RAJYA SABHA [8 MAY, 2000] 
exception of USA, for phasing out these QRs USA filed a dispute against India 
in WTO and the Dis pute Settlement Panel ruled against India. India filed an 
appeal before the Appellate Body of WTO against the findings of the Panel but 
the Appellate Body also upheld the findings of Panel. Both these Reports were 
adopted by the Dispute Settlement Body (DS B). Consequently, a bilateral 
Agreement was signed between India and USA for determining the reasonable 
period of time for implementing the rulings and recommendations of DSB. As 
per the Agreement, QRs on 714 items have been removed with effect from 1 -
4-2000 and QRs on remaining 715 items are to be removed by 1-4-2001. 
USA is not maintaining any Quantitative Restrictions on imports on 
account of Balance of Payments reasons . However, USA maintains import 
restrictions on textile products in form of 'quota'. As per the Agreement on 
Textile and Clothing of WTO, all members including USA are obliged to remove 
these restrictions in a phased manner. These restrictions are to be completely  
removed by 1-4-2005. 
Apprehensions have been expressed in certain quarters r egarding the 
adverse impact of import restrictions removal on 714 items on domestic 
producers. These fears are premature, as the imports are being closely monitored 
and government would strive to ensure, through appropriate use of tariff 
mechanism that imp orts do not cause any serious detriment or injury to the 
domestic industry. 
The Special Economic Zone scheme announced in the new export-import 
policy is a WTO compatible scheme, which has been widely welcomed by all, 
including various state governments. Proposals have been received from some 
of the state governments for setting up such zones in their states.

96 

[8 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING AND MINISTER OF STATE OF THE 
DEPARTMENT OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY) : (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
(b) Disinvestment in Public Sector Enterprises is a continuous process 
that was initiated in 1991 to provide market discipline to the performance of 
Public Enterprises and to promote greater accountability in them.  Later in 
1996, the policy provided for the examination of the question of withdrawing 
the Public Sector from non core strategic areas, to establish a Disinvestment 
Commission to advise on disinvestment and to implement decisions to disinvest 
after considering the advice of the Commission. The disinvestment policy 
after 1998-99 provides for bringing down Government equity in all non strategic 
Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) to 26% or lower, if necessary and also to 
restructure and revive potentially viabl e PSUs, close down PSUs which can 
not be revived and to fully protect the interest of workers. The withdrawal of 
the Public Sector Enterprises from non strategic areas would not be automatic 
and would depend upon whether the industrial sector requires the presence of 
the public sector as countervailing presence to prevent strengthening of power 
in private hands and whether the industrial sector requires a proper regulatory 
mechanism to protect the consumer's interest before Public Sector Enterprises 
are privatised The policy is thus a judicious mix of withdrawal of tax payers 
money from volatile markets and strengthening the public sector where 
necessary. The policy would ensure better use of human and other capital 
assets in the Public Sector Enterprises an d more competition in each sector. 
The tax-payers money released through disinvestment would be used in higher 
priority programmes like health and education, retiring of Government debt 
and for restructuring and strengthening identified PSUs.

4498. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD : Will the Minister of SOCIAL

(a) whether Government are considering any proposal to bring 
unorganized sector under pension scheme;

(d) if so, the salient features thereof ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) The salient features of the report of the Expert Committee are as 
follows :—  
(i) The Project OASIS (an acronym for Old Age Social & Income 
Security) Expert Committee submitted its report to the Ministry of 
Social Justice & Empowerment in January, 2000. The Committee 
has recommended a system which can be used by unorganized sector 
workers spread all over India, which enables them to attain old age 
income security at the price of modest contribution rates through 
their working career. 
(ii) The proposed system is based on Individual Retirement Accounts 
(IRA).   A person will open a single IRA with the proposed system 
125 

RAJYA SABHA [8 MAY, 2000] 
at as early a point in his life as possible. The account will provide the 
individual with a unique IRA number that will stay with the individual 
through life. The individual would save and accumulate assets into 
this account in his working life, subject to a minimum of Rs. 100 per 
contribution and Rs. 500 in total accretions per year. Individuals 
would be free to decide the frequency of accretions into their accounts; 
there will be no pressure to make a fixed monthly contribution. The 
account would stay with the individual across job changes, spells of 
unemployment, and can be accessed at any location in India. The 
individual would always have access to an account balance statement 
showing his assets. All through, the individual would be empowered 
in having control of how his accumulated assets should be managed. 
Finally, upon retirement, the individual would be able to use his

4508. SHRI GANDHI AZAD: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that adequate share of budget for the development 
of SC/ST/OBC and minorities Welfare Schemes in proportion to their percentage 
of population has not been provided; and 
(b) if so, what are the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI): (a) and (b) It is 
a fact that allocation of funds for development of SCs/STs/OBCs and minorities 
is not in proportion to their population. The Planning Commission is of the 
opinion that "population" alone cannot be taken as the sole criterion for allocation 
of funds for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, OBCs and Minorities 
development. 
137 

RAJYA SABHA [8 MAY, 2000] 
However, Special Component Plan (SCP) and Tribal Sub-Plan (TSP) have 
been in operation since 1979-80 for supplementing/complementing the Central 
and the State budget for development of SCs and STs. In terms of this 
arrangement, population is the major criterion to assist the quantum of funds 
under various development sectors both at the Central and the State leves. 13 
Central Ministries and 24 States/UTs are successfully implementing these two 
strategies. 
Special Central Assistance (SCA) is being provided by Central 
Government as an additionality to SCP and STP budgets in the State Sector. 
Population is the major criterion for allocation of funds for this purpose. 
Besides, in order to encourage substantial allocation of resources, Central 
Assistance is also being provided under Article 275(1) of the Constitution for 
improving the infrastructural facilities in the Tribal areas.

Production cost of Steel 
†4514. SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV : Will the Minister of STEEL be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the unit-wise production cost of steel; 
(b) the total amount of tax imposed on steel; 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
142 

[8 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the average market price of steel; 
(d) what is the percentage of profit therein; and 
(e) the steps taken to reduce the prices of steel ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI 
DILIP RAY): (a) to (e) After the decontrol of steel in January 1992, the 
demand, production and prices of steel are driven by market forces. The cost 
of production of steel primarily depends upon prices of inputs such as iron 
ore, coal, steel scrap and energy, cost of freight and labour Customs/Excise 
Duty on inputs and raw materials and financial charges. The cost of these 
inputs factors keeps varying from time to time according to the inter -play of 
market forces. The cost of production also varies from item to item and 
depends on the specification thickness, grade etc. of the steel items required 
to be produced. As such an average cost of steel production cannot be arrived 
at. Moreover the Government has no role to play in either fixing the prices of 
steel or in the profit margin. The Government's role is limited to levying of 
taxes on steel and as per budget 2000 -01, th e Central value added tax has 
been proposed to be fixed @ 16% and the peak rate of custom duty has been 
proposed to be levied @ 35%.

THE MINISTE R OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) to (d) The 
increasing trend of population also results in pollution problems. To control the 
problem Government has brought into force the following Acts :—  
(i)   Water (Pollution Prevention & Control) Act, 1974 
(ii) Air (Pollution Prevention & Control) Act, 1981 
(iii) Environment (Protection) Act, 1981 & 1986 
The Ministry of Environment and Forests has taken several steps to control 
pollution in major cities as per details in the Statement [See below]. 
Further, Government has adopted the strategy of development of rural 
areas (through various schemes), small and medium towns and satellite towns

Statement 
* Effluent and emissi on standards have been notified under the 
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to check pollution. 
* Highly polluting industries have been directed to install necessary 
pollution control equipment in a time bound basis and legal action has 
been initiated against the defaulting units. 
* Under the World Bank Scheme, 89 Common Effluent Treatment Plants 
have been provided subsidy, which are at various stages of 
implementation. 
* Environment Impact Assessment Notification, 1994 is in force 
governing environmental apprai sal of 29 specified categories of 
developmental projects. 
* For control of pollution from vehicles, emission norms for both petrol 
and diesel driven vehicles at the manufacturing stage were introduced 
for the first time in 1990 and made tighter in 1996. More  stringent 
emission norms will come into effect, from 1-4-2000.

a number of retail outlets in Delhi and Mumbai to cater to the CNG 
fitted vehicles

been drawn up for restoration of environmental quality in these areas. 
* Action Plans for control of pollution in Delhi and Mumbai are being 
implemented A decreasing trend in Air pollution has been obse rved 
recently in Delhi and Mumbai due to various pollution control measures 
taken by the Government.

economically useful public assets. This programme targets the urban poor who

was also permitted to divert and utilise available unspent fund s from one 
component of SJSRY to another based on local needs.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Correcting the Statement made on 13th March, 2000 to Starred 
Question 309 answered in the Rajya Sabha on 20th December, 1999 
regarding anti-dumping duties investigations 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
MURASOLI MARAN): Mr. Chairman, Sir, with your permission, I will read 
this correction. The Customs Tariff (Identification, Assessment and 
Correction of Anti -Dumping Duty on dumped article s and for determination 
of injury) Rules 1995. empowers the Central Government to impose anti -
dumping duty. The designated authority appointed by the Government in 
accordance with this rule, investigates the existence, degree and the effected 
alleged dumpi ng in relation to import of any article and recommends the 
amount of anti-dumping duty, which if levied, would be adequate to remove 
the injury to the domestic industry. The Central Government, i.e. the 
Department of Revenue. the Ministry of Finance, may impose, by notification 
in the official gazette, duties as recommended by the designated authority. 
The correction, therefore, is to specify the recommendations of the 
designated authority and the rate of duty imposed by the Central 
Government. Thank you, Sir.

SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would 
like to supplement what Shri Shatrughan Sinha has said about our people in 
Pakistani jails. Whether it is the Pakistanis in Indian jails or it is the Indians 
in Pakistani jails, we know what the international law is. We are humanitarian 
people. We are reasonable people. Therefore, we have to make our stand very 
clear that there is no Pakistani in our jails. I would like to refer to what Col. 
KM. Pattu, the Working President of the Missing Defence Personnel 
Relatives' Association, has said. He has said, "The Geneva Convention calls 
for release and repatriation of prisoners without delay after ceasession of 
hostilities. It also calls for Commissions for the purpose of searching 
dispersed PoWs and assuring their repatriation with the least possible delay." 
He also adds: "There is  no record available to us proving that India 
constituted such a commission either to trace the missing Indian soldiers in 
Pakistan or to assure Pakistan, in a transparent manner, that there were no 
Pakistani soldiers in India." I would like to request the  Government to 
constitute this commission at least now, even though 25 to 30 years have 
gone by, so that the world knows whether we have any soldiers as prisoners 
in our jails. If we do have them as prisoners, we should release them. Or else, 
we can let th e world know that we really do not have any prisoners. Why I 
am saying is, - we have our experiences in the recent Kargil war as well as in 
the war of 1971 - the families of a number of prisoners, in their letters written 
way back, have stated that they wi shed that their family members had better 
died in the war than for them to know that they are alive but are not traceable. 
If they had died, at least, the Government would have recognised their bodies 
and handed them over to their families.  But when 
192 

RAJYA SABHA [8 MAY, 2000] 
they are alive, they are being taken away by the Pakistani authorities. And 
the Governments of India -  both the earlier Governments and the present 
Government - have not done enough to bring them back to their family 
members. Sir,  I don't want to add to what Shri Shatrughan Sinha has 
mentioned. I don't want to repeat the names either, except for one name, 
namely, Captain Ravinder Kora, whose existence was proved as late as 1991. 
What have we been doing since the last 10 years? So, Sir, I would only say, 
unless we deal with the prisoners in a transparent manner, it would only 
show that the humanitarian feelings of our Government, of our country, have 
been completely reduced to zero. We are talking of the senior officers of the 
Army who had been working for the safety and integrity of our country. 
Once they are found missing, nothing is done to bring them back to the 
country. Sir, I would once again request the Government to do something in 
this regard. I would also request you, Sir, to direct the Government to 
institute this commission and to inform the House within a time -limit as to 
what steps they have taken in this matter. 
SHRI N. THALAVAI SUNDARAM (Tamil Nadu): Sir, it appears that 
there are nearly 295 Indians in the Pakistani jai ls. Recently, 90 fishermen 
were released from the Pakistani jails. All the belongings of these fishermen 
have been confiscated by the Pakistani authorities. And, these fishermen 
had stated that there are more than 210 army personnel in the Pakistani jails 
and that they are living in a very bad condition. Before these fishermen 
were released, a group consisting of Members of both the Houses met them, 
and we were informed that there were nearly 295 Indians in the Pakistani 
jail. Sir, there are Pakistani soldiers in our jails also. So, unless some 
dialogue takes place between India and Pakistan on this matter, we cannot, 
really, solve the problem. The Army personnel are there in Pakistani jails 
for more than 15 to 20 years. So I request the Government to take n ecessary 
action to get all the Indians released from the Pakistani jails. Thank you, 
Sir.

Non-Payment of Wages to Casual News Readers of All India Radio 
 
PROF. (SMT.) BHARATI RAY (West Bengal): Sir, through you, I 
would like to bring to the notice of this  august House, a case of injustice. 
Sir, the News Services Division of All-India Radio, New Delhi, has long 
195 

[8 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
been running largely by casual news readers on contract basis. These casual 
news readers perform all duties assigned to regular news readers. They face 
all hardships and even on all occasions like Holi, Republic Day and 
Independence Day, they perform duties. The news unit of the New Delhi 
station runs on a skeletal staff. The English unit has only nine permanent 
staff, agai nst 150 people on the casual panel. In the Bengali unit, there are 
only two regular staff, against 15 casual news readers. The ratio is almost 
1:15. It is difficult to believe, but it is true that these casual news readers have 
not been paid their dues fro m June, 1999. It is a year now. We are in May. 
Everyone expects money for the work done. If you take the service, then you 
need to pay. If you can't pay, then do not take the service. That is the general 
rule. But, in this country, in the national capital itself, in one of the most 
powerful media centres of our country, this simple rule is being violated. I 
understand that when the casual news readers approached the authorities, they 
were told that it was up to the Prasar Bharati. But the Prasar Bharati, in  turn, 
pleaded resource crunch. If there is no money, then why do you have their 
service? How can you keep the people waiting for a year for their dues? 
I would like to bring another interesting point before the House. The 
casual news readers are being pai d only Rs. 150 for the past ten years. After 
the Fifth Pay Commission's recommendations, it was increased to Rs. 225. 
After three months, by an order, it was restored to Rs. 150. Sir, as you know, 
All-India Radio is an important organ which caters to the m edia, needs of 
millions and millions of people in the urban and rural areas. The TV, 
certainly, is a more powerful medium, but it does not reach all. On the other 
hand, the All -India Radio caters to all and it has a much bigger clientele. 
Thousands of people, in India, particularly, in the rural areas, are familiar with 
current issues, with the problems and achievements of our country, only 
through the News Services Division of All -India Radio. The news . readers, 
therefore, render an important service to t he nation. They should not be 
victims of injustice. I appeal, through you, to the concerned Ministry to look 
into the matter. I demand that the dues should be paid in lumpsum, not in 
instalments. Justice needs to be done to all, irrespective of class, cast e, gender 
or category of work. 
Free Flow of Fake Currency Notes and its Impact on the Economy 
PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM (Tamil Nadu):   Mr. Chairman, Sir,   I 
wish to bring to the notice of the Government the free flow of fake currency 
196 

RAJYA SABHA [8 MAY, 2000] 
notes of Rs.500 and Rs. 100 denominations in our country. This free flow of 
fake currency notes really cripples the economy of our country. We have 
come across news reports that Samjhauta Express is a channel through which 
fake currency notes of Rs .500 denomination are entering in our country. I 
insist upon the Government to take effective measures for stopping this free 
flow of fake currency notes of Rs.500 and other denominations. It is 
understood that most of the nationalised banks when they come  across some 
fake currency given by a customer instead of reporting the matter to the 
concerned authorities for taking appropriate action they themselves alert the 
man who brings that currency by saying, "You will be put to trouble. You 
tear off this note. " They themselves tear such a note into two or three pieces, 
give it to the customer, and advise him to be careful in future. This type of 
thing in the nationalised banks would not help the concerned and appropriate 
forums to find out the source of this cu rrency. So, necessary circular and 
instructions have to be sent to the nationalised banks. If the Government 
officersor anyone who come across this kind of currency, they should inform 
the concerned persons and the concerned Department for taking action. B ut, 
what they say is that if they inform the concerned authorities, then they have 
to face the harassment of the inquiry officers; they have to go to the court; and 
they have to face the music. The Government must find out a way to avoid 
such type of a situation. At the same time, I wish to bring to your notice, Sir, 
that the Government has announced that they are going to release Rs. 1000 
denomination currency in the very near future. Even now it is difficult to 
distinguish between the notes of Rs. 100 and Rs.500 denominations. An 
ordinary man is not able to differentiate these denominations. Only s slight 
difference in size is not sufficient. I heard a telecast distinguishing the fake 
currency and the genuine currency. I very closely followed it but even now I 
have not been able to understand it. So, only this type of a thing will not be 
sufficient to educate people to differentiate between the fake and the real 
currency notes. Moreover, if the Government is thinking of issuing Rs. 1000 
denomination notes, they must change the sire and colour elaborately.   At 
least, this point should be taken into consideration. 
A few months back, it was reported that a school in south Delhi had 
come across a fake currency note while collecting fees from the students. We 
do not know as to what has happened to that case. I would like to know whether a 
case has been registered in this regard.     We do not have any 
197 

[8 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
information in this regard. So, I request the Government to keep all these 
things in mind and take effective steps and measures to arrest this free flow of 
fake currency notes into our country. Otherwise, it will ruin the economy of 
our country as some of our enemies are determined to do it. If there are 
currency notes of Rs. 1000 denom ination, it will further tempt the anti -social 
elements. Therefore, before issuing the currency notes of Rs. 1000 
denomination, the Government must take all these things into consideration. 
It should be done in such a way that it helps our country. With these words, I 
finish my submission.

DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA (Assam): Mr. Chairman, Sir, thank you 
very much for giving me this opportunity to associate myself with this 
Special Mention. The issue of fake currency is a very serious threat to the 
economy of our country. It has a serious impact on our economy. The 
machine used for detection of fake currency is out of reach of the common 
man. That is one of the reasons that fake currency is being circulated 
throughout the country, especially in the North- Eastern region. I am laying 
emphasis on the North -Eastern region because I represent that area. The 
North-Eastern region has become a dumping ground for fake currencies. 
There is sufficient proof that the ISI is involved in dumping of fake 
currencies in this region. Last year, there was a news item in different 
newspapers that the ISI is pouring a huge quantity of fake currency from 
abroad into the North -Eastern region. Another dimension of the problem is 
that there is an acute shortage of fresh currency, new notes in the North -
Eastern region. For the last 4-5 years, the RBI has not replaced the old, soiled, 
unhygienic, depleted notes, in the region. Sir, it reflects on the prestige of the 
country. I have got samples of these old, soiled, unhygienic, depleted notes 
with me. The hon. Finance Minister is also here; I would like to show these 
notes to this august Ho use. Such notes have not been replaced for the last 4 -5 
years. These are still in circulation. Some of the notes are even beyond 
recognition; as to which denomination do they belong; whether they are one -
rupee notes, or two -rupee notes, or five -rupee notes . Even the fifty -rupee 
notes are in a very depleted condition. I hope, the hon. Finance Minister will 
take adequate steps to direct the RBI to replace all such soiled notes. If a 
tourist comes to India and handles such type of notes, it reflects on the ima ge 
of the country. I hope, the Finance Ministry would take this matter seriously 
and would see that these notes are be replaced immediately.

SHRI SH ANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY (West Bengal): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, 1 associate myself with the Special Mention made by hon. 
Smt. Saroj Dubey. This reflects the problem of rehabilitation. We have a 
growing urban sprawl.  It is not confined to Delhi alone, but it is also there 
204 

RAJYA SABHA [8 MAY, 2000] 
throughout the country. I would urge the Government that it must not only 
take the proper, short -term measures that the hon. Members have pointed out 
but it must also have a look at the long -term economic policies, by which 
industries, particularly under the new regime, the liberalised regime, are 
being concentrated in those favoured areas where the so -called infrastructure 
exists. Unless industries are dispersed and the means of livelihood are created 
in villages,this flow to cities will continue. India is a country where 80 per 
cent of the people live in the villages. It is also a forecast that within the first 
quarter of this century, up to 30 per cent of our people will be living in 
towns. So, I urge the Government t o bear this in mind. Please not only plan 
for the short -term, immediate measures to be taken but also, on a long -term 
basis, see that, with the industrial policy you are following, the centres of 
growth are spread throughout the country and ensure that a d egree of 
humanism is there when encroachments are vacated. 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa): Sir, I associate myself with the 
Special Mention made by Smt. Saroj Dubey. 
The first point I want to make is that there should be, in such cases, no 
eviction without settlement, and the settlement should be at a place where the 
poor people, the miserable people who live in slums, have employment 
oportunities. These words are mild, compared to the words used in the 
National Housing and Habitat Policy. I have this document here with me. 
This document was brought out by this Government in furtherance, as it 
says, of the NDA's National Agenda for Governance. It states here in the 
very first paragraph: 
'Mere  lip-service  will  not  do.     What  is  required  is  a housing 
revolution." 
Is this the housing revolution? When people do not get houses and 
when their wives and children do not have even the foothpath to live on, they 
go and occupy land and build their own shelter. This is happening not only in 
this country but all over the world. The policy makers at the global level have 
a global consensus that this is something which is a human problem. There 
should not be eviction without proper settlement. This is a global consensus 
which exists everywhere in Asia, in Africa and in  Latin America, in 
particular. This is point number one. 
Secondly, why are people living in slums? 
205 

[8 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
The Minister is here. That is good. The Minister will reply to this, and I 
will be very happy. 
People live in these miserable conditions. This Housing Policy says: 
" 'Like beasts' words even beasts would protest." 
That is what the housing policy says in the very first paragraph. Why 
are our co -citizens living like this? They live like this because there is no 
employment. Basically, this is the result of the migration of people from rural 
areas to urban areas. What is happening is that in rural areas, employment 
opportunites are falling completely. The development is decreasing. In the 
1980's, the rate of growth in the rural areas was 3.1 per cent, as per the 
Planning Commission. Now, in the last couple of years, it has been 1.8 per 
cent. Now, the employment is decreasing to such an extent that when the 
Congress left the Government in 1995- 96, the rural poverty was 38 per cent, 
and it has now grown to 45 per cent. I am mentioning about the rural poverty. 
I am quoting the figures given by the Member of the Planning Commission, 
Dr. S. Gupta, in public, a couple of months ago. This is the position. 
Therefore, the first thing that is req uired is to increase the number of houses. 
You say here, if I am not mistaken, in paragraph 1.7 of this document: 
"Two million units will be created, built by the year." 
I want to know from the hon. Minister what progress has been made in 
this regard. 
Number two, in this Budget, the allocation for rural development, 
everything concerning rural development, the Rural Development Department 
itself, has been slashed down in a manner which, I feel, is brutal. There is a 
sharp slashing down of all projects of ru ral development, including self -
employment and employment in the rural areas. That is why these things are 
happening. Therefore, we have to pay attention to the fact, that this imbalance 
which is growing between the rural areas and the urban areas in terms  of 
growth, development and employment, is growing very fast because of the 
manner in which our new economic policies are being implemented. 
Therefore, I appeal here to the Government: 
Number one, increase your Budget allocation for the Government 
programmes for employment in the rural areas at a faster rate. 
206 

RAJYA SABHA [8 MAY, 2000] 
Number two, increase the housing, particularly the housing for the poor 
people. Let us see what you have done about your plan for 2 million units per 
year. The hon. Minister will be able to tell this to us. 
Number three, please implement what you say here in the beginning of 
paragraph 5.7 of the Policy. You say: 
"Slum improvement/upgradation" 
Instead of improving and upgrading the facilities which are practically 
nil in sl ums, you are just destroying them and sending the people away. 
There is a sharp contradiction between the words and the action on the 
ground. Therefore, I request that these things should be done. The first thing 
is: No demolition without proper settlement. 
Thank you.

up any such notification and express his view, and if a Member of Parliament 
picks it up, then, a Statutory Resolution is moved by the Member. 
Once it is moved by the Member and then admitted and taken up by the 
House, the House has to express its views. So far as the present notification is 
concerned, the present scheme is concerned, it has been stated that it will 
have to be laid on the Table of the House and the Minister has done that. This 
scheme was amended on 20th January. This scheme was laid on the  Table of 
the Lok Sabha on 10th March. This scheme was laid on the Table of the 
Rajya Sabha on 14th March. I have no dispute on that; I have no quarrel. The 
Government has complied with that part of the requirement, but where, to my 
mind - and I am subject  to correction by the Minister - the Government has 
failed is where they have already put it into operation, after making the 
amendments on 20th January. The interpretation of the law, according to me, 
that Government should have waited till the completion  of 30 days. If 
Parliament had not taken notice of it, it would have been assumed that 
Parliament had agreed to it and there was no need of bringing it. Sir, in this 
connection, I would also like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister to a 
case in which the Supreme Court had given a judgment. It is civil appeal No. 
4247 (50 of 1996) decided on 13.3.1996, New Bank of 
219 

[8 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
India Employees' Union versus Union of India, where it has been stated and I 
quote only the relevant portion , "whereas under the Banking Regulation Act 
Scheme framed as merely to be placed before the Parliament and nothing 
further, but under the Acquisition Act, the scheme becomes effective only 
after the same is placed before both the Houses of Parliament and a fter the 
Parliament makes such modifications and agrees to the scheme. In this view, 
the matter of the decision of this court in supra case whether simply by 
modifying the scheme can the Government make it operational from the day 
of the Gazette notification.' In this the relevant date is 20th January, 2000. 
This is one point on which I would like to seek a clarification from the hon. 
Minister. 
The second point on which I would like to seek a clarification from the 
hon. Minister is, why this scheme was passed. Umteen number of discussions 
have taken place. Umpteen number of court cases have been filed. In the 
spirit of nationalisation, in the spirit of taking control over the nationalised 
banks, it was suggested, as it was pointed out, when the Nationalisation Bill 
was piloted by the then Prime Minister on the floor of the House and on the 
floor of the other House, that an institution which serves, subserves, the 
largest interest of the people be brought within the control of the people 
through the representa tives of the people in various schemes. In a number of 
judgments - one thing has been quoted by my friend, Shri Dipankar 
Mukherjee - it has been pointed out that an institution, like bank, must, in its 
policy formulation, in its administration -  not day -to-day administration, of 
course; that will be left to the executive, but in the policy formulation - must 
represent the cross -section of the interest of the people. That is why it was 
suggested that one per cent - this will be nominated by the Government - is 
there to protect the interest of the defaulters. There must be a Chartered 
Accountant, there must be a representative of the workmen, there must be a 
representative of the employees, there must be a representative from the 
Reserve Bank of India, Governm ent representatives. Normally, the Ministry 
sends a representative to the nationalised banks at the level of the Joint 
Secretary or some other appropriate level. 
Six persons should represent various interests. I have no quarrel. The 
Government of the day c an decide as to who will be in a better position to 
represent which interest. That prerogative lies with the Government. It is for 
the Government to decide as to who will be nominated. Surely, I can't raise a 
220 

RAJYA SABHA [8 MAY, 2000] 
question on that . But in regard to two representatives, representing the 
workmen and employees, an elaborate scheme was worked out as to how 
they will be chosen. Where there is a representative union, you can decide 
which representative union is in a position to send it. The Government 
accepts it and then they will have the priority. If there is no representative 
union then what has to be done? All these things have been elaborated in the 
scheme itself. This elaboration clearly demonstrates that the Government is 
keen to have the right type of representative of the workmen and the right 
type of representative of the employees of the bank. They should also 
participate - you talk of management culture wherein employees and others 
also would participate in it. It is true that because of certain factors, the 
constitution and reconstitution of the Board of Directors has taken an 
unusually long time. It took a long time even during our time also. For that, I 
am not blaming the Minister. But, at the same time, this job is to be don e. 
When it is to be done, I expect the Government to come forward, if they want 
to have a scheme, if they want to improve the same. Surely, nobody would 
like to argue that what was decided twenty years back is sacrosanct. If the 
Government of the day consi ders that with the changing situation, certain 
amendments, certain modifications, certain changes, in the scheme are 
necessary, by all means, they have got a right to do so. 
What I want to point out is, the Government should have explained the 
scheme to th e Parliament; and, after explaining it to the Parliament, if you 
want to implement it, there will be no problem. This is one area where 
everybody is interested. On an earlier occasion, the other day, while replying, 
it was pointed out that the Government w as not going to just denationalise 
the banks and the Government was contemplating on bringing fresh capital; 
and, in that process, the Government was going to invite private sector capital 
also. But there was no question of disinvestment straightaway by re ducing 
the Government's share. If I understand the Minister correctly, he explained 
like that. But there is a lot of talk going on; and, in that process, when a large 
number of bank directors are changed, in 20 banks, naturally, it creates a lot 
of confusion. You have a right to put the type of persons whom you feel can 
represent various interests in the best manner. The law gives you this 
authority. The statute of the scheme, its real implication, according to my 
understanding, is to be laid on the table o f the House; not merely for 
increasing the academic interest of the Members, but because if some 
Members consider it necessary to have a pointed and 
221 

[8 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
focussed discussion, he can resort to the provision of Statutory Resolution 
and bring it to the notice of the House, invite comments and response from 
the Government and, thereafter, the House can decide. 
Therefore, I would request the Government, especially the Finance 
Minister, to give us an assurance that he will bring out a co mprehensive 
scheme, in tune with the changing situation and take both the Houses into 
confidence, discuss the scheme and, thereafter, implement and operationalise 
the scheme. If this is done, I think, the attention, which the mover wanted to 
draw of the Government, would be served. 
I do feel that this legal position should also be clarified. It can be 
interpreted that this matter can be taken up in detail by the Subordinate 
Legislation Committee of both the Houses. Since this is brought in the Rajya 
Sabha, it should have been taken up here in the Rajya Sabha. I request the 
hon. Minister to give an explanation as to what is the impact of the Supreme 
Court judgment, where they have interpreted that this particular act as a 
legislative act. 
If it is so, then wh at would happen? Of course, there is a provision, a 
saving clause that in between if the Parliament nullifies that does not mean 
what action has been taken from 20th January till date will be nullified. That 
action will remain intact. Normally saving provi sions are provided in every 
clause. But, what I feel is that there was no need of a great hurry or urgency. 
For several years these Boards have not been constituted. If you want to have 
a scheme, if you have a better scheme, a better idea, if you want to b ring 
changes which are required in the changed situation, by all means, you do 
that. But, before implementation, you please take the House into confidence 
and bring your proposal or scheme so that we have an opportunity to examine 
it, to scrutinise it. With these words, 1 stand by my motion.

Sir, the other general point, which I would like to make in the 
beginning, is that this action of the Government has been challenged in the 
Delhi High Court, and the matter is, in a way, sub -judice. The next date is 7th 
July. I think as far as  the legal validity of this action of the Government is 
concerned, the Court will pronounce its judgement in due course. But, 
through you, Sir, I would like to take the House into confidence and say what 
exactly we have done. What we have done is, under the scheme which has the 
status of a subordinate legislation under the law, we have deleted a certain 
expression which appeared in brackets. It said that a non -official director will 
continue as a director until his successor had been appointed even after hi s 
three-year term, for which he had been appointed, came to an end. We are 
aware that the bank has some official Directors and some non -official 
Directors. According to the present scheme, the representatives of the 
workers and the representatives of the O fficers are also treated as non -official 
directors. Now, some directors had been appointed in 1995 at the time when 
the Congress was in power. They completed their three- year term. Then in 
April 1998, unfortunately, it took us a little time, and it is taki ng us a little 
time, not for the reasons which Mr. Salim has mentioned, but for an entirely 
different reason. Even the Congress Government, which came into office in 
1991, had appointed these Directors in 1995. So, it takes a little time. It is not 
because there is an Alliance in Government today or because there was one 
party in Government. Let us not look for reasons where reasons do not exist. 
It has taken us a little time. What happens is, when the thee year term comes 
to an end, then a Member of the Bo ard, who is a non- official Director, lives 
almost from day -to-day, because the moment the Government makes an 
appointment, his term will come to an end. I personally felt that this was not a 
very right kind of an arrangement that they should continue on al most a day-
to-day basis. Therefore, we put our heads together and decided that we 
230 

RAJYA SABHA [8 MAY, 2000] 
should bring their tenure to an end, by an amendment of the scheme. On 20th 
January this year we amended the scheme. Because the workmen -director 
and the Officer -director were also in the category of non -official directors, 
they also had to go under this arrangement. It is not that we were holding 
something against them. It is not that we are not aware of their value or we 
want to keep them out b ecause the financial year was coming to an end. It 
was merely because the non -official directors' tenure had to come to an end 
through this notification. 
Now, an issue has been raised by Pranab Babu in regard to its being laid 
on the Table of the House or the Government having to wait for 30 days 
before giving effect to it. We have already gone into it in detail. I would like 
to mention that there had been similar amendments earlier also which had 
been given effect to immediately, like we did now. I have co me across 
another formulation for this. This is the Industries (Development and 
Regulation) Act, 1951, where there is a similar provision. There it is 
mandatory to take the approval of the House. It talks in terms of a draft 
notification, not a final notif ication. So, the legislation is very careful in 
choosing its words. The present Act does not talk of a draft legislation. It 
talks of notification as such. As I said, this is the principle that we have 
followed in this case. In giving effect to it, I had to come to this House and 
lay it on the Table of both the Houses. This is what I have done. There is a 
provision in sub -section (6) of Section 9 of the Banking Companies Act 
which says that it will be laid and, within 30 days, hon. Members have a right 
to m ove amendments, like it has been done today. But it also says very 
clearly that even if the notiication is amended, as Pranab Babu has said, 
whatever action is taken will be saved. Action will be taken only if the 
notification comes into effect. Otherwise there will be no action. If we wait 
for 30 days, as, under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, we 
will wait for 30 days. 
There will be no action because the notification will not take effect. In 
any case, I am not like many distinguished Members of this House. I am 
neither a legal expert nor a distinguished lawyer. But I would like to say that 
all these are issues which will be decided in a court of law. In the Delhi High 
Court, we will defend the position of the Government. 
Now, in regard to the other issue which had been raised by Pranab Babu 
about the new scheme, we are aware that the scheme which has been in force 
231 

[8 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
  since 1970, was amended in 1980 and 1988 and on various occasions. This 
scheme has also a provis ion regarding reduction of government equity in 
bank. For instance, let us say, we will bring it down by 20 per cent. Then, two 
out of these six Directors will be elected by the shareholders. If it goes down 
by another percentage, then, it will be further reduced and there will be four 
directors. If it is 20 to not less than 40 per cent, then, four Directors will be 
elected by the shareholders. Where it is more than 40 per cent which is the 
case in some banks, then all the six directors, non -official directors, will be 
elected by the shareholders. This is also part of the scheme. So, I agree 
entirely with Pranab Babu that this whole thing needs to be looked at afresh. 
What was valid, let us say, 30 years ago or 20 years ago, may not be valid 
today. Things ha ve changed, circumstances have changed, and I have come 
before this House and I will come again. I have explained, and Pranab Babu 
has quite rightly interpreted this, that the announcement that I have made in 
this year's Budget speech that we will bring do wn wherever necessary, we 
will have an enabling provision in the Bank Nationalisation Act to bring the 
equity below 50 per cent in Government. I will come before this House and 
that will be the occasion when we will be looking at provisions relating to the  
board of directors as well because there are certain issues to which the 
Government would like to apply its mind. For instance, whether all the 
directors, non -official directors, should be elected by the shareholders, 
whether the Government should not ret ain the right to nominate some people, 
these are issues which will have to be very carefully considered. So, a totally 
fresh new look at the whole scheme is very much on the agenda of the 
Government. When I come with my legislative amendment of the Banking  
Nationalisation Act, I will be coming with necessary amendments in regard to 
this scheme also. 
On the point raised by Mr. Virumbi, I think the total number of directors 
who went out as a result of the action of Government was 127. I would like to 
say that  I myself would like to put the officer -director and the workman-
director in a separate category so that there is no discontinuity as far as they 
are concerned. Even the procedure today is extremely complicated. It is a 
very complex procedure. Whenever a v acancy is likely to arise, we approach 
the Chief Labour Commissioner in the Ministry. The Chief Labour 
Commissioner then goes and makes a verification of the membership of the 
various unions in the banks to find out which is the union which has the 
majority, which should, then, make a suggestion in regard to

this and submit a panel. Then the union which is so selected submits a panel 
of three people. Then the bank management sends us a whole lot of other 
material. They send it  to the RBI. It is a very long drawn out procedure. 
When we take a fresh look at it, we would like it to be streamlined so that the 
delay part between one and another is taken care of as quickly as possible. 
That is, as I said, Sir, very much on the agenda . The Government has 
absolutely no ill-will in bringing this. We want the boards of directors of the 
banks, as I have said on earlier occasions in this House, to be as professional 
as possible so that banks function along professional lines. The financial 
sector is extremely important for the economy of our country. And there is no

have done it with the best of intentions, we will continue to act with the best 
of intentions in the bes t interest of the banks, in the best interest of the 
financial sector as a whole and in the best interest of the national economy. 
With these words, therefore, I would most earnestly plead with the hon. 
Members that in view of the clarifications that I hav e offered, they might 
consider withdrawing the Statutory Motions. Thank you.

giving me this opportunity to express my views on the Appropriation B ill 
presented by the hon. Finance Minister for consideration of the House. This 
is the final stage or the penultimate stage of the consideration of the Budget

broad functioning of  this Government in the last year and also try to assess 
the direction into which this Government wants to move in the coming 
financial year. 
At the same time, Sir, I would like to draw the attention of the House, 
and also the attention of the hon. Finance  Minister, to certain aspects which 
need to be looked at because, after all, the Budget estimates are only a means 
to carry out the governance of this country. The whole gamut of economic 
and financial activities of this Government, in my view, veers round  to what 
is now come to be known as globalisation or liberalisation or economic 
reforms. I am not against either of these, in principle, but it would be prudent 
in my view that while we take one step forward or while we take any step 
forward, we should pau se and think as to what impact that measure or that 
step would have on the broad mass of the people of this country, who still 
constitute the weaker sections, the poorer sectors and those living below the 
poverty line. 
We have said; and we commonly use a metaphor "reforms with a human 
face". There is no dispute about this metaphor, but that this metaphor does 
not become a meaningless metaphor is something which we have to look at. 
That is something which not only we, but, I am sure, the Government also 
would like to look at . While everyone in this country, and also in this House, 
appreciates the pioneering spirit of the great leaders for making the industrial 
revolution in this country- and you can take the name of some leading 
people~we must also clearly un derstand that the face to which reference has 
been made cannot be the face of these great captains of the industry. That 
face, Sir, will have to be the face envisioned by none else but the Father of 
this nation, and that face, Sir, is the face of Daridranarayan, in all his pathos 
and simplicity. Every step that is taken must, therefore, conform to his 
interest, must serve his interest, and, I think, you remember that on the 
morrow of independence, Gandhiji gave a talisman to this nation, specially to 
those in whom the nation entrusted the responsibility and the authority to 
govern. It was a simple talisman that all those who exercise authority in the 
name of the nation must, at all times, before they take an

action which affect s the millions of his countrymen,   pause and consider 
whether that step adds or subtracts to the burden of the Daridranarayan.

have added to the woes, anxieties and burdons of the common man. When I 
say this, I am not trying to prescribe anything. But I am only sounding a note
